chunks: Rijal al-Kashshi: Hamduwayh and Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Khayran al-Khadim who said:

I sent to my master eight dirhams and wrote to him: I have sent you eight dirhams which had been gifted to me from Tarsus, dirhams from them [non-Muslims]. I disliked returning them to their owner, or doing something new with them without your command. Do you order me to accept their like or not? So I may know it, if Allah wills, and it reaches your command. So he wrote and I read it: Accept from them if dirhams or other than them are gifted to you, for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did not return a gift from a Jew or a Christian. He said: And I said: May I be your ransom … He said: Act in that according to your opinion, for your opinion is my opinion, and whoever obeys you has obeyed me.

key_terms.طَرَسُوسَ: Tarsus (a city in the Roman Empire)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on accepting gifts from non-Muslims in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Rijal al-Kashi* highlights the Imam al-Jawad’s (AS) pragmatic approach to social interaction with Ahl al-Kitab, affirming the permissibility of accepting their gifts as a means of fostering goodwill (*mu'atara*). The Imam’s declaration that 'your opinion is my opinion' underscores the concept of *ijtihād* within the household of the Prophet, granting the servant delegated authority to make contextual rulings. This incident serves as a key precedent in Shia jurisprudence for the ritual purity of non-Muslims' possessions and the validity of their gifts.
